subject: Canada's 3% inflation is really a gas price story
bodyMarkdown:
Statistics Canada said on Monday that consumer prices rose 3% in August, the same pace as July. Almost all of the distance between that number and the Bank of Canada's 2% target is sitting in your gas tank, which changes what the number should mean for your mortgage.

## What the August numbers actually say

The headline is 3%. Underneath it, gasoline was up 22.8% from a year ago, and that one line is doing most of the lifting. The Bank of Canada's two preferred measures of **core inflation**, which trim away the most extreme price moves so you can see the trend underneath, came in at 1.9% for trim and 2% for median. That is target. Groceries actually cooled, rising 2.8% after 3.1% in July, and by Statistics Canada's count it was the first month since July 2024 that food from stores rose more slowly than prices overall. Shelter ticked up to 1.5% from 1.3%, with rents at 2.8%. The economy families live in and the economy the Bank steers by are giving different readings, and the gap between them is a barrel of oil.

## Why Macklem is sitting still

The Bank held its policy rate at 2.25% on September 2, its seventh straight decision without a change. CBC reported that Governor Tiff Macklem said inflation risks had sharpened since July, with global oil prices persistently high and no end in sight to the conflict in the Middle East. He also said the new American duties would weigh on fourth quarter growth and hit targeted sectors hard, without a large direct impact on the wider economy. I read that as a central bank that has decided to look through the pump. Raising rates cannot refill a pipeline or reopen a shipping lane, and the pain would land on mortgage holders who did not cause the problem. What he is really watching is whether Canadians start treating 3% as normal, because expectations are the part of a supply shock that monetary policy can actually reach.

## Washington may go the other way tomorrow

The Federal Reserve announces at 2 p.m. Eastern tomorrow, and traders think it raises. CNBC reported on August 28 that the September decision had become a coin flip after hawkish signals from new Fed chair Kevin Warsh, and Yahoo Finance reported this month that odds of a quarter point increase had climbed past 60% on CME FedWatch, which infers probabilities from fed funds futures prices. That would be the first American increase since 2023. If it lands while Ottawa holds, the rate gap between the two countries widens, and money follows the higher rate. The loonie has been trading near 72 cents US, and money.ca reported it sliding to 72.25 cents after an August jobs report that showed Canada shedding almost 42,000 positions while the United States added 162,000. A cheaper dollar makes everything Canada buys in US dollars dearer, which is how a decision in Washington reaches a grocery bill in Richmond Hill.

## The takeaway

Watch 2 p.m. tomorrow, and watch the loonie more closely than the rate itself, because the currency is how an American hike gets imported here. If you have a renewal coming, Monday's print gave the Bank no reason to cut and no reason to hike, so plan around 2.25% instead of waiting for relief that the data does not support. The number I will be checking next is the core pair in the October 19 release, since trim and median drifting above 2% would mean the oil shock has stopped being temporary and started being inflation. Until that happens, 3% is mostly a Middle East story wearing a Canadian price tag.
